newsitem.title: USA: Dollar mixed after mark, gains against yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed after mark, gains against yen.

text.p: The dollar fell against the mark Monday as investors flocked to the German currency on news that British Prime Minister John Major was calling a general election.

The prospect of political uncertainty in Britain, where Major's ruling Conservative Party lags the opposition Labour Party by more than 20 points in opinion polls, prompted traders to sell British pounds for marks.
Lingering uncertainties about the timetable for a single European currency also helped buoy the mark, pushing it higher against other European currencies.
The dollar rose against the weakened pound and also edged higher against the Japanese yen.
Analysts said dealers were still optimistic about the dollar's prospects, adding that the highlight of the session was renewed mark strength rather than dollar weakness.
"Today's dollar losses are not a sign of any newfound bearishness against the greenback" but of stronger demand for the mark, said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"People are still optimistic on the dollar over the long-term and this is just a correction in the uptrend," he said.
The dollar stood at 1.6910 marks in late New York trading, down from 1.6950 marks at Friday's close. The dollar edged up to 123.74 yen from 123.50 late on Friday.
The British pound slid to $1.5887 from $1.6013.
The dollar edged higher to 1.4590 Swiss francs from 1.4575 on Friday and rose to Canadian $1.3700 from $1.3653 at Friday's close.

Major announced Britain's general election will be held on May 1. Ahead of the announcement, election jitters sparked heavy selling of pounds for marks, widely viewed as a haven in times of political uncertainty in Europe.
Comments from German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who said that strict adherence to criteria for the single currency was more important than meeting the 1999 timetable, also buoyed the mark.
Doubts about prospects for a single European currency tend to strengthen the mark at the expense of other European currencies because the mark has less to gain from the project.
The dollar gained against the yen despite news that Japan's trade surpolus had risen 6.5 percent year-over-year in February, the first rise in 27 months.
"That says that underlying sentiment to the dollar was not all that negative or they would have seized on the (figures) to sell," Chandler said.
Trading was generally subdued with many investors hesitating to take large positions ahead of the next week's meeting of Federal Reserve policy-makers.

The market is divided on whether the central bank policy-makers will raise interest rates in a bid to head off inflation. A rate hike would tend to benefit the dollar by making dollar-denominated assets more attractive.
